actions.justification: Mandatory first step: patient is tachycardic (HR 105) with hematemesis/melena, suggesting active upper GI bleed. Hemodynamic assessment is critical to determine severity and resuscitation needs.
Mandatory assessment of vital signs to establish baseline and monitor for hemodynamic deterioration in the setting of acute GI bleed.
Mandatory: large-bore IV access required for fluid resuscitation and potential blood product administration in active GI bleed.
Mandatory: CBC to assess hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet count in a patient with hematemesis and melena to evaluate degree of blood loss and anemia.
Mandatory: Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) to evaluate for coagulopathy in the setting of upper GI bleeding.
Mandatory: Type and crossmatch to prepare for potential blood transfusion in this patient with active GI bleeding (hematemesis and melena) and tachycardia (HR 105).
BMP is needed to assess electrolytes, BUN/creatinine ratio (elevated in UGIB), and renal function to guide resuscitation and risk stratification.
Repeat CBC to trend hemoglobin given ongoing hematemesis and melena; initial CBC may not reflect true blood loss due to hemoconcentration.

Patient has tachycardia (HR 105) with hematemesis/melena indicating active GI bleeding. IV crystalloid bolus is indicated to support hemodynamic stability while awaiting blood products and further workup.
GI consult is mandatory for urgent endoscopy in a patient with hematemesis and melena; endoscopy within 24 hours (ideally within 12-24h) is standard of care for UGIB.
IV proton pump inhibitor (e.g., pantoprazole) is indicated early in suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding to reduce rebleeding risk and facilitate clot stability.
Patient has tachycardia (HR 105) despite fluid resuscitation; lactate will help assess degree of tissue hypoperfusion and guide resuscitation adequacy.
Patient with hematemesis/melena and HR 105 is at risk for significant blood loss; type and crossmatch is needed to prepare for potential transfusion if Hgb returns low.

Prokinetic agent (e.g., erythromycin or metoclopramide) given before endoscopy improves gastric visualization by clearing blood from the stomach, improving diagnostic and therapeutic yield of upper endoscopy in upper GI bleed.
Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) reduces splanchnic blood flow and is indicated empirically in upper GI bleeding, particularly if variceal bleeding is suspected, while awaiting endoscopy.

Serial CBC is needed to trend hemoglobin in this patient with active upper GI bleeding (hematemesis and melena) and tachycardia. This will determine if transfusion threshold (Hgb <7) has been reached.
Trending lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation in this GI bleed patient who remains tachycardic, to identify occult hemodynamic compromise.

Patient has active GI bleeding with tachycardia. Per evidence-based guidelines for upper GI bleeding, packed RBCs should be administered if hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL. This conditional action is appropriate to initiate now pending CBC results.

Patient with hematemesis and melena at 90 minutes with tachycardia (HR 105) and active GI bleeding requires surgical consultation in case endoscopic therapy fails or if there is evidence of ongoing/massive hemorrhage requiring surgical intervention. GI has been consulted; surgery should be involved early for potential operative management.

CT abdomen can help identify the source and extent of GI bleeding, assess for complications such as perforation, and guide further management when endoscopy findings are pending or equivocal. Patient is currently hemodynamically stable (BP 120/80, MAP 73) allowing for imaging.

Patient presenting with hematemesis and melena with persistent tachycardia (HR 105) despite resuscitation measures already completed. Angiography can identify the source of GI bleeding and potentially allow therapeutic intervention (embolization) if endoscopy is not feasible or has failed. This is the only available action in the current phase and is clinically appropriate for ongoing upper GI bleeding workup.

Per GI bleed guidelines, upper endoscopy (EGD) is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for hematemesis/melena. GI has been consulted and patient has been stabilized with octreotide and PPI - endoscopy should proceed to identify and treat the source of bleeding (variceal vs non-variceal).
